summary: Specifies a minimum set of requirements for Uniform Resource Names (URNs), a kind of resource identifier that stays the same even when the resource moves. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: A name that stays the same for a thing even if its address changes, like a person's name versus their home address.

subtitle: The minimum requirements for a name that identifies a resource forever, whatever happens to where it lives.

tldr.problem: Internet resources can move, be copied or disappear, so a location-based name does not work as a lasting identifier.
tldr.mechanism: The memo lists functional requirements (global scope, uniqueness, persistence, scalability, legacy support, extensibility, independence, resolution) and encoding requirements for Uniform Resource Names, and draws conclusions about naming authorities.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational basis for evaluating URN standards. It deliberately leaves resource equality, visible name semantics and name resolution to others.

today: RFC 1737 is an Informational memo from December 1994 and does not specify a standard. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: URNs in the Information Architecture
sections.content:
The memo specifies a minimum set of requirements for Uniform Resource Names (URNs), meant as a basis for evaluating URN standards. URNs sit beside Uniform Resource Characteristics (URCs) and Uniform Resource Locators (URLs): URNs identify, URCs carry meta-information such as owner, encoding, access restrictions or cost, and URLs locate.

A URN identifies a resource or unit of information. A URL identifies a place or container where an instance may reside, which is different from the resource itself. A resource named by a URN may be in several places, may move, or may not be available at all. The memo sums up the purpose of a URN as a globally unique, persistent identifier used for recognition, for access to characteristics of the resource or for access to the resource itself.

The requirements are not exhaustive. Replication and security issues were discussed but were not well enough understood to include specific requirements.
sections.plainLanguage: A name tells you who something is. An address tells you where it is right now. A URN is the name, so it keeps working even if the thing moves.

sections.title: Functional Requirements
sections.content:
The memo lists eight requirements on what a URN must be able to do:

  • Global scope: the same meaning everywhere, and no implied location.
  • Global uniqueness: the same URN is never assigned to two different resources.
  • Persistence: the lifetime is intended to be permanent, even beyond the life of the resource or of any naming authority.
  • Scalability: usable for any resource that might conceivably be on the network, for hundreds of years.
  • Legacy support: existing systems such as ISBN numbers, ISO public identifiers and UPC product codes seem to satisfy the functional requirements and should be embeddable.
  • Extensibility: future extensions must be possible.
  • Independence: only the name issuing authority decides when it issues a name.
  • Resolution: a URN must not impede translation into a URL, and where URLs exist there must be a feasible mechanism to translate.
sections.plainLanguage: A good lasting name must mean the same thing everywhere, never be handed to two things, and last a very long time. It also has to let you find where the thing lives.

sections.title: Encoding Requirements
sections.content:
Six further requirements cover how a URN is written as a string. There is a single encoding for people and for transmission. Comparison is simple: one local, deterministic algorithm that needs no external server. URNs should be transcribable by humans, which means short, few special characters and case insensitive; the memo says there is no strong requirement that people can generate or interpret them.

A URN must be transport friendly, passing unmodified through protocols such as TCP, SMTP, FTP and Telnet and onto paper. It must be machine parseable, and its encoding should make it easy to find and parse in free text.
sections.plainLanguage: The name has to be easy to copy by hand, easy to put in an email, and easy for a computer to spot in a paragraph of text.

sections.title: Implications: Naming Authorities
sections.content:
To meet uniqueness and scalability, name assignment is delegated to naming authorities, who may assign names directly or hand authority to sub-authorities. Each authority guarantees uniqueness for its names. The names of authorities are themselves persistent and globally unique, and top level authorities will be centrally registered.

Scalable naming schemes are encouraged but not required. A mapping from each authority's names to URLs is strongly recommended, with zero or more URLs for a URN at any time, though the authority itself need not provide it. The character set must be limited so URNs can be transcribed and mailed, but there was not yet consensus on the limit.
sections.plainLanguage: To keep names from clashing, a few big offices hand out name ranges, and each office makes sure it never gives the same name twice.

sections.title: Issues Left Open on Purpose
sections.content:
The memo takes no position on three issues: how equality of resources is judged, whether visible meaning is built into a URN, and name resolution. Each authority must use one equality algorithm, but different authorities may differ. A publisher might tell printings of a book apart where a library would not.

A naming authority may embed knowledge in names (as ISBN numbers do) or not, for example by issuing monotonically increasing serial numbers. The memo allows the whole range but says authorities should be discouraged from exposing semantic information about the resource, since it may change over time. On resolution, it only recommends that each authority have a name translation mechanism and encourages third-party and distributed resolver services.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo does not decide when two things count as the same, or how to look names up. It leaves that to whoever hands out the names.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The security section is short. Applications that translate names to locations, and the resources themselves, may require authentication. The memo says information about authenticating the name or the resource should generally travel as separate information alongside the URN, not inside the URN.
sections.plainLanguage: If you need proof that a name or a thing is genuine, send that proof separately instead of hiding it inside the name.

viz.caption: THE EIGHT FUNCTIONAL REQUIREMENTS FOR URNS (RFC 1737)

items.title: Global scope
items.text: Same meaning everywhere; no location implied.

items.title: Global uniqueness
items.text: Never assigned to two different resources.

items.title: Scalability
items.text: Any resource, for hundreds of years.

items.title: Legacy support
items.text: ISBN, ISO public identifiers and UPC codes can be embedded.

items.title: Extensibility
items.text: The scheme must allow future extensions.

items.title: Independence
items.text: Each issuing authority sets its own conditions.

items.title: Resolution
items.text: Must not impede translation to a URL.
